rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible while revealing the full retention window and any strongly compressed regions. This balances coverage and run time, giving a useful first map of where to narrow the gradient and whether later runs should focus on slope or temperature.

All peaks eluted well within the gradient, so trimming the solvent window to the observed elution window should preserve full elution while reducing the time penalty. Keeping tG and T fixed isolates the effect of the narrower phi range and may improve spacing around the crowded 5–8 min region.

The broad window was clearly better, so now test slope directly by halving tG while keeping phi and temperature fixed. This will show whether the critical mid-run cluster benefits from a shallower or steeper gradient and may improve CRF by shortening the run if resolution remains acceptable.

The 10 min gradient is fastest but over-compresses the critical 5–8 peak cluster, while 20 min fully resolves it but costs too much time. An intermediate slope should retain the zero time penalty yet recover resolution for the (5,6) and especially (6,7) pair.

The limiting pair improves strongly with shallower slope, and 14 min already gives a near-optimal score with no time penalty. A small increase to 16 min should further separate the critical pair while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve the zero time term.

The main unresolved issue is the stubborn (6,7) pair, and its strong dependence on tG suggests we are near the time-resolution tradeoff optimum at 14 min. A modest temperature decrease may shift selectivity enough to open that pair while keeping the run within the no-penalty time region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction at the same near-optimal slope. A modest increase to 45 C could shift selectivity favorably for the crowded central cluster while likely preserving a zero time penalty.

With tG limited to 2 min steps, the unresolved tradeoff is whether the gain in the critical pair continues enough beyond 16 min to outweigh extra time. Testing 18 min maps that curve so we can bracket the optimum more confidently around the current best region.

The best score is at 14 min and the last peak still elutes far before the gradient ends, so a slight reduction of phi1 may tighten the useful gradient window without the severe retention increase seen at phi1 0.65. This tests whether a modestly narrower window can improve selectivity in the crowded center while keeping the run in the zero-penalty region.

The slight narrowing from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF, suggesting the gradient window is better matched to the actual elution range. One more step lower in phi1 should test whether the critical central pair gains further selectivity before retention becomes too long.

At phi1 0.90 the method is near-optimal and still has no time penalty, but the limiting pair remains only modestly resolved. A slightly steeper gradient may reduce total time enough that any small loss in resolution still improves CRF, while also testing whether the narrowed window changes the slope optimum relative to the 0.95 runs.

At phi1 0.90, 12 min is too steep and 14 min is excellent, so the key remaining question is whether a slightly shallower slope resolves the limiting pair enough to offset any added time. This directly probes the local optimum around the current best method on the improved phi window.

The best method is now well localized, so use remaining budget to search for a selectivity gain at the best phi window and slope rather than chasing slope further. Since both 35 C and 45 C worsened selectivity at phi1 0.95, testing a larger temperature shift on the improved 0.90 window could still reveal a favorable reordering effect for the critical pair.

Temperature perturbations are clearly unhelpful, so return to 40 C and test whether raising phi0 slightly improves spacing in the crowded middle by shifting the effective phi window upward while keeping the favorable phi1 and tG. The first peak is still well retained, so phi0 0.10 should be safe and may sharpen the tradeoff around the critical pair.

Raising phi0 improved CRF, and at phi0 0.05 a modest reduction in phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 was beneficial. Combining both trends by narrowing the upper end slightly at the new best phi0 may give just enough extra selectivity for the critical pair while keeping the run under the no-penalty threshold.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this injection should explore robustness immediately around the optimum rather than chase a higher score. Increasing phi0 one step tests whether the method sits on a broad plateau or whether the current optimum is sharp, while keeping all other successful settings fixed.

Since the optimum appears to lie on a plateau, continue mapping that plateau by raising phi0 one more step while keeping the proven upper bound and slope. This checks how far phi0 can be increased before the earliest peak becomes effectively unretained or central selectivity deteriorates.

The best region is clearly around phi0 0.10–0.15 with phi1 0.85, so now test a slightly narrower upper end at the better of those starting conditions. This checks whether the CRF=1.000 plateau extends to an even tighter window or whether phi1 0.85 is already the lower useful limit.

The CRF=1.000 plateau includes phi0 0.10 and 0.15 at phi1 0.85, and lowering phi1 to 0.80 at phi0 0.15 nearly preserved it. Testing phi0 0.10 with phi1 0.80 maps the lower-left corner of that plateau and may retain perfect score with slightly different retention distribution.

The 1.000 region appears centered near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, so testing the complementary upper side at phi0 0.15, phi1 0.90 completes the local plateau map. This will show whether the optimum is broad in phi1 at the better starting strength or whether 0.85 is the true sweet spot.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, use the remaining injections to test robustness against faster gradients at one of the tied best solvent windows. This checks whether the optimum is tolerant to a shorter tG or whether 14 min is uniquely required for full resolution term at the winning composition.

Repeat the faster-gradient robustness test at the other tied-best solvent window to see whether phi0 0.15 better tolerates steeper slope than phi0 0.10. This helps define whether the CRF=1.000 plateau has a preferred center if a shorter method were ever desired.

With the maximum score already found, use one of the last injections to test temperature robustness directly on a winning solvent program. A 5 C decrease checks whether the optimum is stable to common operating variation or whether selectivity around the critical pair is sharply temperature-sensitive at the best composition.

A lower temperature badly perturbs selectivity at the winning solvent program, so use the penultimate run to test the opposite temperature direction on the other CRF=1.000 method. This completes the practical robustness picture around the optimum while avoiding repetition.

For the final run, probe the best-resolved nearby variant by combining the stronger central-pair separation seen at phi1 0.80 with a slightly shallower slope. This tests whether a hidden alternative optimum exists adjacent to the CRF=1.000 plateau, while the confirmed best methods remain 0.10/0.85/14/40 and 0.15/0.85/14/40.
